經過了不懈的努力與一次又一次的啾啾啾後，
洛克人又又又又一次從威力手中守護了世界和平。
合輯2的內容包含7代到10代四款元祖洛克人，
老實說在玩過畫面相對漂亮的7、8代後，
9、10代又回到象素風畫面是有點無法接受的，
像這樣逐代玩下來能感覺到時代的進步也是一種樂趣。
7代的隱藏要素非常豐富，拜現在網路發達所賜，
知道了很多以前玩的時候完全沒發現的內容。
親手重現時有種莫名的感動，也再一次體會到，
7代除了畫面以外蘊含了多少製作組的誠意，讓人慶幸能再一次玩到。
8代因為以前沒有ps，合輯版是我第一次玩到。
遊玩下來感覺畫面整體非常有動感，能購買的零件也很好玩，
只可惜零件不可能全部購買。不過滑雪的部分就不太推了...
9代復古的畫面如果是讓人有點小失望的話，a
把洛克人的滑壘和集氣拔掉就真的無法接受了。
不過關卡上能感覺出很費心思設計，以復出作來說我覺得算及格。
這代開始能夠玩老哥布魯斯，簡單說就是完整版的洛克人，
有集氣和滑壘，外加跳躍時有盾防禦，但是被打傷害和擊退2倍，
算是高手向角色。
10代除了多一個佛魯迪以外感覺跟九代比沒什麼變化，個人感覺不好不壞。
另外多提醒一下，除非對身手有自信，不要想不開拿布魯斯打困難模式...
我打完當下第一個想法是"終於結束了..."，
體會到的比起成就感更多的是解放感，大概絕對不會用布魯斯玩困難第二次了吧。
這代的挑戰關卡是每代遊戲各玩各的，相比合輯1代數混合起來會好打很多。
除了STEAM成就外，9代10代本身也有各自的成就，有興趣可以挑戰看看。
雖然有大概4分之1不太如人意，但總的來說是值得洛克人迷購買的作品。

コレクション2に収録されているロックマン7〜10は、1〜6とは明確に異なる立ち位置のナンバーだと思っています。
完成された傑作群である1〜6を踏まえた上で、新しいハードへの挑戦、シリーズを打破しようとする試行錯誤、そういったチャレンジ精神が前面に出た時代の名作たち。どの作品からも、汗と努力と熱意が伝わってきます。洗練され切ってはいないかもしれませんが、その分、作り手の「模索」も味わい深い、楽しいナンバー群です。

■ロックマン7
ワイリーカプセルがシリーズ屈指の強敵と言われがちですが、実際にはアイテム交換や道中の取得によってE缶4個＋M缶1個というフル装備で挑める設計になっています。つまりこれは理不尽なボスではなく、総力戦として用意された最終決戦。資源をすべて注ぎ込んで押し切る白熱したバトルが楽しめます。
ステージ道中は、途中からスーパーロックマンで無双できるため、見た目ほど難易度は高く感じません。新要素を余さず楽しめる一方、ロックマンや敵のサイズが大きく、画面がやや窮屈に感じる点は好みが分かれるかもしれません。
あとBGMはOP・タイトルからEDまでどれも良いと思います。

■ロックマン8
アローショットという、着弾後に炸裂する新バスターがとにかく爽快です。撃って気持ちいい、キャラの声がついて楽しいポップな印象のロックマン作品です。
強化パーツを変更することで、2周目以降もプレイ感が変わり、繰り返し遊べる作りになっているのも魅力です。
ただし、新要素のスノーボードは場違いなほど鬼畜。「ジャンプ、ジャンプ、ジャンプ、ジャンプ、スライディング、スライディング、ジャンプ……」という悪夢の指示ボイスが脳内再生され、毎晩うなされる覚悟は必要です。

Mega Man 7

The first game in the collection. MM7 is a REALLY good game and a fantastic debut in the 16-bit era. I made the mistake back in the day to keep comparing it to Mega Man X "there's no dash," "this game feels slow," "not as cool without Zero in it," etc, but in reality, MM7 is a 16-bit game that plays just like an 8-bit NES game, and it does that perfectly. Once you understand that, you'll start to appreciate the game for what it is. I was a bit surprised by the amount of secrets the game has, so there's definitely opportunities to replay levels—and maybe you'll find a super cool easter egg. That said, if upgrade hunting isn't your thing, the shop is back and offers the possibility to buy energy tanks, weapon refills, lives, and some of the upgrades, though not all of them.

In my opinion, the only thing bad about MM7 is the intro cutscene, and that's it. You're forced to watch a 2-minute  cutscene every time you start a new playthrough, but it also sets a cheerful tone and welcomes you to the 16bit era graphics. The rest of the game is freaking fantastic—literally a love letter to everything cool about the classic series: beautiful sprites, enjoyable level design, good music, and Bass's debut. The Robot Master designs are a highlight on their own; they are all quite good. Also, MM7 is where we first see Robot Masters weaknesses really shuts them down in the classic series, they literally get stunlocked and/or stuck in a single pattern. They definitely took a page from Mega Man X but dialed it up to 11 (no pun intended). Be warned though, MM7 showcases the hardest final boss in the whole classic series —words directly from the devs, so blame Inafune. 
Oh, and Proto Man is back, kinda psycho, telling you about burning down forests or something. Huh.

Once I beat the game, I read around to see what the general consensus about the game was, and apparently some people had problems with Mega Man's sprite size. I actually never noticed, I just thought it was part of the art style, but it's something you'll get used to anyway, and it doesn't affect gameplay at all. There is also a retro TV filter that makes the game look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful with sharper pixels.


Mega Man 8

MM8 felt like a grand welcome to the 32-bit era. The graphical leap was obvious, with plenty of experimental stuff too and visual flavor in every single stage—though I'd argue the visual clutter sometimes was a bit too much. It's something you just get used to.

Overall, the game is packed with little details that enhance the experience: either the presentation, sprite animations, stages variety, the exposition with anime cutscenes, or the art direction in general (something MM8 really excels at). It all comes together in a charming package full of personality, especially with the Robot Masters and their banter dialogues.

I thought the soundtrack was something straight out of Marvel vs. Capcom, but apparently MM8 came first, maybe such compositions were part of that Capcom era. Speaking of which, this was the time of Capcom's cringy dialogue and weird voice acting (looking at you, Resident Evil), and honestly, I love it. Their games had that charm in their attempt to push the experience forward, and inadvertently set an industry standard, for better or worse.

One extra tip: the first power you get in the tutorial is the the Mega Ball. The game never tells you that you can bounce off it and used it to reach high places (it works a lot like Rush Coil, which isn't in this game), or even use it to jump repeatedly mid air without apparent limit besides the weapon's ammo. Although this requires practice and a small sense of timing, it's absolutely worth learning. That might have been explained in the game's manual, but there's no such thing in the digital version.

After finishing MM8, I came to the realization this game has a reputation of being the black sheep of the classic series—some people don't like the art style, others the way Mega Man controls, or any nitpicks in between. This was my first playthrough, and in my experience, that reputation is completely undeserved. Props to Capcom for trying new stuff, like the new types of Mega Buster for example. Some mechanics might work while others are left behind (swimming or the limited bolts currency in this case), but creativity is what this game excelled at, and without it, there is no innovation. I admit Mega Man felt slightly slow at first, but then again the sentiment faded the more I played. One culpript might be the default slide, which by the way you can upgrade in the shop to reach longer distances and make the gameplay much better.

As a last note, MM8 is a game full of charm. The difficulty is more in favor of the player, so you can have a good time even if you are not that fond of the challenge level in the classic series. There is one exception with the inclusion of a couple of sidescroller segments that require some precise timing, but fortunately the checkpoints let you retry immediately. Lastly, the voice acting was a product of its time and is one of those things that can be remembered with nostalgia and make you laugh.


Mega Man 9

Personally, this was the tittle I was more excited about when I first started playing the collection—a curious return to the classic NES style.

First things first, if you like Mega Man 2, you are going to absolutely love this game. At least I know I did. You might as well call it Mega Man 2-2; the overall feeling is extremely similar to the second entry of the franchise.

The graphics might seem "old," but it was a deliberate choice to make the game look and feel exactly like the early games in the series. In fact, since it was a choice instead of a product of hardware limitations, the game has some nuances that are not present in the NES games. No slowdowns whatsoever, super tight controls, vibrant colors, and tons of details in every level that enhance the visual experience—whether it's backgrounds, basic enemies, or mid-bosses. Pretty impressive for a "NES game"

Immediately starting the game, you see the beautiful sprite artwork and some of Capcom's classic quirkiness while they explain the plot. Unlike Mega Man 7 and 8, there is no intro stage this time—you go straigth to the stage select screen. The shop is back too, with a solid amount of helpful items and what you'd expect.

But it all boils down to whether you love or hate the gameplay. Like I said, MM9 is a throwback to the NES titles, especially MM2. Simply put, Mega Man can not slide or charge his Mega buster, and as surprising as that sounds, I really don't think it's deal breaker—especially since the game was designed around this style of gameplay. 

Although we are back to the simple "jump and shoot" formula, the levels feel tight and compact. Pretty much every screen has something going on, which helps keep the fast pace of the game. The challenges are creative and fun—like jumping portals, platforms that roll and unroll like snails, or swinging platforms that play with physics.

Traps are fair; they don't feel brutal or punishing, just more like "pay attention" moments. Even if you die, you are never too far from the action thanks to how easily the stages flow. However, If I remember correctly, there are about 2 or 3 precision jumps in the whole game—two involving those swinging platforms and maybe one more in the endgame. 

There are two playable characters: Mega Man and Proto Man. Coincidentaly, Proto Man can slide and charge his Proto Buster. There's a caveat, though: Proto Man receives double damage and is only playable after beating the game, or you can use a code to unlock him right away. Just note that there's no separate story if you play as him.

The game difficulty felt a bit harder than the rest of the classic games—not punishing, but just hard enough to be considered an enjoyable challenge to veterans of the franchise.

And lastly the music—a perfect return to the catchy songs that we all love.

[h1]TL;DR / Verdict[/h1]

Overall, this collection is worth it for the games alone, especially on sale, but you could very well get a better experience through emulation. That said, these are still quality titles that I enjoyed, and at the very least, I [b]highly recommend Mega Man 8[/b].

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Mega Man 7[/h1]

I didn’t really enjoy this one. At best, I’d say it was okay.

My biggest issue is the visuals. I really don’t like the sprite art or pixel work on the SNES. Mega Man feels way too big on the screen, and that directly hurts how the game feels to play. Compared to the NES entries, he feels slower, heavier, and far less maneuverable, which makes movement and platforming less satisfying overall.

The item design is another major step back. The way upgrades are hidden feels poorly thought out, especially the reliance on Rush Search. Certain items are forcibly locked behind it, with little to no indication that you’re missing something important. That led to a lot of unnecessary level replays, which felt frustrating rather than rewarding.

Compared to Mega Man 6, this honestly feels like a step back. Exploration often felt like trial-and-error rather than clever discovery.

There were other smaller issues too, but they all fed into the same core problem:
[b]this game just doesn’t feel as good to play as the earlier entries.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Mega Man 8[/h1]

Mega Man 8 feels like a full correction of the missteps I had with Mega Man 7.

The gameplay is noticeably tighter and far less weighty. While Mega Man is still on the slower side, his proportions are handled much better here—he no longer feels screen-dominating or awkward to maneuver. Movement and dodging feel more natural and readable, which makes the game feel far more fair and responsive.

Visually, this is a massive upgrade over 7. The sprite work is beautiful, the animations are expressive, and everything feels properly scaled. The jump to PS1 hardware also allows the soundtrack to shine, with more depth and richer instrumentation. This is easily one of my favorite Mega Man OSTs in the entire series.

Stage design is another highlight. Levels feel more creative overall, with gimmicks that enhance the experience rather than hinder it. Sword Man’s stage in particular stands out as one of the most memorable and inventive in the classic series.

The Robot Masters themselves are also far more imaginative. Tengu Man and Sword Man are two of the coolest designs I’ve seen so far, both visually and mechanically.

My only real complaint is Mega Man’s overall speed. He feels slow enough that the game can sometimes feel longer than it needs to be, especially during backtracking or extended stages. Still, this is a minor issue in an otherwise excellent experience.

Overall, Mega Man 8 is a fantastic entry. It fixes nearly every problem I had with Mega Man 7 and could easily be my favorite Mega Man game, or at the very least second only to Mega Man 6.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Mega Man 9[/h1]

Mega Man 9 is… fine. And honestly, that’s kind of disappointing.

On a mechanical and aesthetic level, it nails almost everything. The music is great, the Robot Masters are creative, and the special weapons are genuinely fun to use. From a presentation standpoint, it succeeds completely at what it sets out to do.

Where the game really falls apart for me is the level design. It leans far too heavily on Mega Man 2 nostalgia, to the point where it feels restrictive rather than respectful. The removal of the slide and charge buster doesn’t add meaningful challenge—it just makes the game feel slower and more irritating to play.

The biggest issue isn’t difficulty, it’s friction. Instant-death hazards are everywhere, and while none of them are especially hard on their own, the sheer frequency makes the experience exhausting over time. Instead of feeling challenged, I mostly just felt annoyed.

I didn’t play the extra content like Proto Man Mode, so this is purely based on the main campaign. As it stands, Mega Man 9 is a game full of great ideas held back by rough, overly punishing stage design.

There’s a lot to admire here, but it never quite comes together into something I love.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Mega Man 10[/h1]

Mega Man 10 doesn’t fix everything I disliked about Mega Man 9, but it’s a noticeably better game, and one I enjoyed much more.

The level design is tighter, the environments feel more creative, and the overall experience is far less grating. The art and music are still great, bosses are fun, and there’s not nearly as much constant friction as there was in Mega Man 9.

My main issues come down to two things.

First, the Robot Master weapons aren’t that great. They work, but most of them aren’t especially exciting or memorable.

Second is how Mega Man and Proto Man are handled. Making Proto Man playable is great, but the execution is frustrating. Mega Man plays like a pre–Mega Man 3 version with no slide or charge shot, while Proto Man gets those abilities but takes double damage and can’t fire multiple pellets. Instead of inventing a unique or interesting moveset, it feels like the game just nerfs one character and shifts abilities between them.

I played most of the game as Proto Man and still had a good time. Mega Man 10 is undeniably a quality entry, but it feels like a game that could have been even better if it pushed its ideas further.
